# 2 Samuel Chapter 16 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 186v–187r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_016_page_001.jpg, 2SA_016_page_002.jpg

---

**1** David had just passed the summit when Ziba, the servant of Mephibosheth, came to meet him. He had two saddled donkeys loaded with two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred raisin cakes, a hundred cakes of summer fruit, and a full wineskin.

**2** "What are these for?" the king asked. Ziba answered, "The donkeys are for the king's household to ride. The bread and fruit are for your men to eat, and the wine is for anyone who collapses from exhaustion in the wilderness."

**3** "And where is your master's grandson?" the king asked. Ziba said, "He's sitting in Jerusalem. He said, 'Today the house of Israel will give me back my grandfather's kingdom.'"

**4** The king said to Ziba, "Everything that belonged to Mephibosheth is now yours." Ziba bowed low. "May I always have your favor, my lord the king."

**5** As King David approached Bahurim, a man came out from the town — a member of Saul's clan named Shimei son of Gera. He came out hurling curses nonstop. **6** He pelted David and all his officials with stones, even though David's soldiers and elite warriors flanked him on every side.

**7** This is what Shimei kept shouting: "Get out! Get out, you murderer! You scoundrel! **8** The LORD is paying you back for all the blood you shed from Saul's family. You stole his throne, and now the LORD has handed the kingdom to your son Absalom. Look at you now — ruined! Because that's what you are: a man soaked in blood!"

**9** Abishai son of Zeruiah said to the king, "Why should this dead dog be allowed to curse my lord the king? Let me go over there and cut off his head."

**10** But the king said, "This is not your concern, sons of Zeruiah. He's cursing because the LORD told him to curse David. Who are any of us to question that?"

**11** David said to Abishai and all his men, "Look — my own son, my own flesh and blood, is trying to kill me. So why be surprised at this Benjaminite? Leave him alone. Let him curse. The LORD told him to.

**12** Maybe the LORD will see how much I'm suffering and repay me with something good in return for the cursing I'm receiving today."

**13** So David and his men continued down the road while Shimei kept pace on the hillside across from them, cursing and hurling stones and kicking up clouds of dust.

**14** The king and everyone with him arrived at their destination exhausted. And there he rested.

**15** Meanwhile, Absalom and all the men of Israel entered Jerusalem. Ahithophel was at his side.

**16** When Hushai the Archite — David's trusted friend — came to Absalom, he cried out, "Long live the king! Long live the king!"

**17** Absalom looked at him and said, "So this is how you show loyalty to your friend? Why didn't you go with him?"

**18** Hushai said, "No — I belong to the one the LORD has chosen, and the people have chosen, and all the men of Israel have chosen. I will stay with him. **19** Besides, who else should I serve if not my master's son? I served your father; now I'll serve you."

**20** Absalom turned to Ahithophel. "Advise us. What should we do?"

**21** Ahithophel said, "Go and sleep with your father's concubines — the ones he left behind to look after the palace. When all Israel hears that you have made yourself repulsive to your father, it will strengthen the resolve of everyone who supports you."

**22** So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the palace roof, and Absalom went in to his father's concubines in full view of all Israel.

**23** In those days, the advice Ahithophel gave carried the weight of a word from God himself. That was how both David and Absalom regarded every piece of counsel Ahithophel offered.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 1-4 — Ziba's opportunism:** Ziba's arrival with provisions looks like loyalty, but it is almost certainly a calculated power grab. By accusing Mephibosheth of harboring royal ambitions (v.3), Ziba positions himself to inherit everything that belongs to his master. David, exhausted and fleeing, makes a snap judgment in Ziba's favor — a decision he will later regret (19:24-30). The narrator never tells us who is lying. We are left, like David, to judge between competing stories with incomplete information.

**Verse 5-8 — Shimei's curse:** Shimei's accusation contains a kernel of uncomfortable truth. David *did* benefit from the destruction of Saul's house, even if he did not orchestrate it. The narrator has been careful to show David's hands clean of Saul's blood, but the political reality is that Saul's fall was David's gain. Shimei names what everyone knows but no one says.

**Verse 10 — "The LORD told him to":** David's response is extraordinary. Rather than silencing his accuser, he entertains the possibility that God is speaking *through* the curse. This is not fatalism — it is a radical openness to divine sovereignty that encompasses even hostile speech. David accepts that God may be using Shimei's hatred as an instrument of discipline.

**Verse 12 — hope in affliction:** Following the Qere reading ("my affliction" rather than the Ketiv "his eye"), David expresses a fragile hope: perhaps God will see his suffering and turn cursing into blessing. This is the theology of the lament psalms — the belief that God attends to the afflicted and that present suffering may be redeemed.

**Verse 22 — the tent on the roof:** The narrator achieves devastating symmetry. David's sin began on a rooftop — when he saw Bathsheba from the palace roof (11:2). Now his son violates his concubines on that same roof. What David did in secret, Absalom does in public. Nathan's prophecy (12:11-12) is fulfilled with terrible precision. The roof is no longer just a location — it is the geography of judgment.

**Verse 23 — Ahithophel's authority:** The narrator's comparison of Ahithophel's counsel to "the word of God" is not flattery — it is setup. If Ahithophel's wisdom is practically infallible, then the only way to defeat it is through actual divine intervention. This is exactly what will happen in chapter 17, when God answers David's prayer from 15:31 by turning Ahithophel's counsel to foolishness.

*— PNEUMA*
